section.title: The River and the Borders of the Land
section.sectionRationale: After all the measured order of gates, chambers, and offerings, the vision suddenly overflows its own boundaries: water trickles from beneath the threshold and, without a single tributary joining it, becomes an uncrossable river that heals the Dead Sea itself and makes trees bear fruit every month. The chapter then widens further still, drawing borders for a land that will even include believing foreigners as full heirs.
section.thesis: Life flows out from the presence of God to heal the deadest places on earth and to make a home for anyone, native or foreigner, who will receive it, a river fulfilled in Christ's gift of living water and consummated in the river of life that flows from God's throne forever.
section.frameNote: Four scenes: the river measured deeper and deeper until it cannot be crossed; the river's life-giving and healing effect on the Dead Sea, its fish, and its fruit trees; the boundaries of the land the LORD gives as an inheritance; and the inclusion of resident foreigners as full heirs alongside the tribes of Israel.

verses.text: Then the man brought me back to the entrance of the temple, and I saw water flowing from under the threshold of the temple toward the east (for the temple faced east). The water was coming down from under the south side of the temple, south of the altar.
Next he brought me out through the north gate and led me around the outside to the outer gate facing east, and there I saw the water trickling out from the south side.
As the man went eastward with a measuring line in his hand, he measured off a thousand cubits and led me through ankle-deep water.
Then he measured off a thousand cubits and led me through knee-deep water. Again he measured a thousand cubits and led me through waist-deep water.
Once again he measured off a thousand cubits, but now it was a river that I could not cross, because the water had risen and was deep enough for swimming, a river that could not be crossed on foot.
“Son of man, do you see this?” he asked. Then he led me back to the bank of the river.
When I arrived, I saw a great number of trees along both banks of the river.

units.label: Everything will live where the river goes
units.note: the Dead Sea made fresh, trees for food and healing

verses.text: And he said to me, “This water flows out to the eastern region and goes down into the Arabah. When it empties into the Sea, the water there becomes fresh.

Wherever the river flows, there will be swarms of living creatures and a great number of fish, because it flows there and makes the waters fresh; so wherever the river flows, everything will flourish.
Fishermen will stand by the shore; from En-gedi to En-eglaim they will spread their nets to catch fish of many kinds, like the fish of the Great Sea.
But the swamps and marshes will not become fresh; they will be left for salt.

Along both banks of the river, fruit trees of all kinds will grow. Their leaves will not wither, and their fruit will not fail. Each month they will bear fruit, because the water from the sanctuary flows to them. Their fruit will be used for food and their leaves for {{marpe|healing}}.”
This is what the Lord GOD says: “These are the boundaries by which you are to divide the land as an inheritance among the twelve tribes of Israel; Joseph shall receive two portions.
You are to divide it equally among them. Because I swore with an uplifted hand to give it to your forefathers, this land will fall to you as an {{nachalah|inheritance}}.
This shall be the boundary of the land: On the north side it will extend from the Great Sea by way of Hethlon through Lebo-hamath to Zedad,
Berothah, and Sibraim (which is on the border between Damascus and Hamath), as far as Hazer-hatticon, which is on the border of Hauran.
So the border will run from the Sea to Hazar-enan, along the northern border of Damascus, with the territory of Hamath to the north. This will be the northern boundary.
On the east side the border will run between Hauran and Damascus, along the Jordan between Gilead and the land of Israel, to the Eastern Sea and as far as Tamar. This will be the eastern boundary.
On the south side it will run from Tamar to the waters of Meribath-kadesh, and along the Brook of Egypt to the Great Sea. This will be the southern boundary.
And on the west side, the Great Sea will be the boundary up to a point opposite Lebo-hamath. This will be the western boundary.

units.label: An inheritance for the foreigner too

verses.text: You are to divide this land among yourselves according to the tribes of Israel.

You shall allot it as an inheritance for yourselves and for the {{ger|foreigners}} who dwell among you and who have children. You are to treat them as native-born Israelites; along with you, they shall be allotted an inheritance among the tribes of Israel.
In whatever tribe a foreigner dwells, you are to assign his inheritance there,” declares the Lord GOD.

marpe.gloss: Healing, remedy, cure. The leaves of the river's trees are for marpe, healing, language Revelation 22:2 draws on directly for the healing of the nations by the tree of life.

nachalah.gloss: Inheritance, a possession given and secured by promise rather than earned. The land falls to Israel as a nachalah because the LORD swore it to their forefathers; the same word frames the priests' portion in chapter 44, where God Himself, not land, is their nachalah.

ger.gloss: Foreigner, sojourner, resident alien. Remarkably, the ger who dwells among Israel and has children is to be allotted an inheritance exactly as a native-born Israelite, a startling widening of belonging within the very same vision that elsewhere restricts entry to the sanctuary.

basic.context: This chapter is the high point of Ezekiel's entire temple vision. A trickle of water seeps from beneath the temple threshold, and as the measuring man leads Ezekiel eastward, it deepens with no tributary in sight, ankle, knee, waist, and finally a river too deep to cross. Wherever it flows it brings life: it sweetens the Dead Sea itself so fish teem in it, and it grows fruit trees on its banks that bear food every month and leaves for healing. The chapter then turns from water to land, tracing the borders of the inheritance the twelve tribes will divide, before closing with an extraordinary widening: foreigners who dwell among Israel and have children are to receive an inheritance exactly like the native-born, treated as full heirs rather than permanent outsiders.
basic.hermeneutics: The river's impossible growth, deepening without any tributary, is the clearest sign in the whole temple vision that this is theological picture rather than architectural plan; a river like this could not exist by ordinary hydrology. Its meaning is unmistakable regardless of how literally or symbolically the surrounding measurements are read: life flows from God's presence outward to heal what is deadest, and that life is offered even to the outsider.
basic.originalLanguages: The leaves of the trees are for marpe, healing, the very word and image John later draws on for the tree of life whose leaves heal the nations, Revelation 22:2. The land comes to Israel as a nachalah, an inheritance secured by God's own oath rather than earned, the identical word used of the priests' portion in chapter 44, where God Himself is their inheritance. And the ger, the resident foreigner, is here promised a nachalah of his own, treated as native-born rather than kept at the margins.
basic.typology: The river flowing from the temple, bringing life and healing wherever it goes, anticipates Jesus' promise of living water flowing from within those who believe in Him, John 7:37-39, and is consummated in the river of the water of life flowing from the throne of God and the Lamb, with the tree of life on its banks for the healing of the nations, Revelation 22:1-2. The foreigner's full inheritance anticipates the gospel's inclusion of the nations as fellow heirs with Israel in Christ.
basic.christ: On the last day of the feast, Jesus stood and cried out, 'If anyone is thirsty, let him come to Me and drink. Whoever believes in Me, as the Scripture has said, streams of living water will flow from within him,' and John explains this of the Spirit whom believers in Him were later to receive, John 7:37-39. Revelation 22:1-2 completes Ezekiel's picture exactly: a river of the water of life, bright as crystal, flowing from the throne of God and of the Lamb, with the tree of life on either side, bearing fruit every month, its leaves for the healing of the nations, the very language of Ezekiel 47:12 fulfilled and consummated.
basic.god: God is the source of all true life; nothing flows from anywhere else in this vision, only from beneath His own dwelling place. He is lavishly generous, sending a river that needs no tributary to become uncrossable, and He is astonishingly inclusive, granting the resident foreigner the very inheritance He swore to Israel's forefathers, a widening of grace that anticipates the gospel going out to all nations.
basic.crossReferences: John 7:37-39 records Jesus' invitation to come and drink of the living water that flows from within believers through the Spirit. Revelation 22:1-2 shows the river of the water of life and the tree of life whose leaves heal the nations, deliberately echoing Ezekiel 47:12. Zechariah 14:8 pictures living waters flowing out from Jerusalem, part of the same prophetic hope. Ephesians 2:12-13 and 2:19 describe Gentiles, once strangers to the covenants of promise, now fellow citizens with the saints, fulfilling the inclusion pictured in Ezekiel 47:22-23.
basic.oneStory: From a river flowing out of Eden to water the whole earth, Genesis 2:10, to a river flowing from a ruined and rebuilt temple to heal the Dead Sea, to a river flowing from the very throne of God and the Lamb at the end of all things, Scripture keeps returning to the same picture: God's presence is the source of all life, and that life flows outward without limit, healing what is deadest and gathering in even the outsider, until at last it reaches its full and final form in the new creation, where God's own dwelling with His people never runs dry.

context.literary:
Chapter 47 has two halves joined by a hinge. Verses 1 to 12 are a vision, narrated in the first person with the guide, and verses 13 to 23 are a speech, introduced by 'This is what the Lord GOD says'. The vision moves by measurement: a thousand cubits, ankle, a thousand, knee, a thousand, waist, a thousand, a river. Each step repeats the same pattern, so the reader feels the deepening, and the guide's question in verse 6, 'do you see this?', slows the pace before the banks and trees appear. The second half also moves by measurement, but of another kind, the borders of the land, and ends on the widening of the heir list to include the foreigner.

The river is the answer to a long absence. Chapters 8 to 11 showed the glory leaving the Temple by the east, and chapters 43 to 46 brought it back and set the rules for living with it. Now what flows out of the house is life. The route is carefully told. Because the east gate is shut, 44:1 to 2, Ezekiel is led out by the north gate and around to the outer east gate, where he sees the water coming from the south side, verse 2. The previous chapters' closed gate is the reason the story takes this detour.

The structure of verses 8 to 12 is a catalogue of life following water. The sea is healed, fish multiply, fishermen stand at the shore, trees line the banks. The exceptions in verse 11, the swamps left for salt, are a deliberate qualification that keeps the picture from being a simple fairy tale.
context.historical:
The river flows toward the Arabah, the great rift valley, and into 'the Sea', which the BSB footnote identifies as the Dead Sea, verse 8. Anyone in Judah knew that water. It lies far below sea level and has such a high salt content that fish cannot live in it. En-gedi, named in verse 10, was an oasis on its western shore, and the idea that fishermen could spread nets there would have sounded impossible to a hearer who knew the coast. The vision therefore takes the most lifeless water in the land and makes it a fishery as rich as 'the Great Sea', the Mediterranean.

The measurement of the river in verses 3 to 5 is a quiet detail. The footnote on verse 3 gives a thousand cubits as roughly 1,750 feet, so four measurements take the man a little over a mile, and the water rises from ankle to swimming depth with no stream joining it. A real river does not behave that way, and the listener would have known it. The impossible growth is how the text signals that the source is the presence of God.

The borders in verses 13 to 20 follow the pattern of Numbers 34:1 to 12 but not exactly. The Transjordan tribes are not given land east of the Jordan; the Jordan is the eastern border, verse 18, and every tribe is placed inside the land west of it. Joseph receives two portions, verse 13, as Jacob had reckoned Ephraim and Manasseh as his own, Genesis 48:5. The southern border runs through the waters of Meribath-kadesh, verse 19, a name that recalled the quarrel of Numbers 20:13.
context.canonical:
The river picks up themes from the whole Bible. Genesis 2:10 speaks of a river flowing out of Eden to water the garden, and the vision places a river at the new Temple, so that Eden's order is restored at the place of God's presence. The psalmist sings, 'There is a river whose streams delight the city of God', Psalm 46:4, and 'You give them drink from Your river of delights', Psalm 36:8. Joel 3:18 says a spring will flow from the house of the LORD, and Zechariah 14:8 says living water will flow out from Jerusalem toward both seas, in summer and winter alike.

The New Testament uses it directly. Jesus cries out at the feast, 'Whoever believes in Me, as the Scripture has said: Streams of living water will flow from within him', and John explains that He was speaking about the Spirit, John 7:37 to 39. At the end of the Bible John sees 'a river of the water of life, as clear as crystal, flowing from the throne of God and of the Lamb', with the tree of life on either bank and leaves 'for the healing of the nations', Revelation 22:1 to 2. The vision has no temple in the city, Revelation 21:22, because the river no longer comes from a house but from the throne itself.

The second half of the chapter is taken up in the story of the land, from the promise to Abraham, Genesis 15:18, to the Torah's borders, Numbers 34, and to Paul's claim that the heirs of Abraham are those of Christ, Galatians 3:29.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Ezekiel wanted his hearers to believe that the same God who had left their Temple would send out from it something stronger than their ruin. The deepest despair in the book is the valley of dry bones, 37:11, and the Dead Sea is its geographical twin, a land of death. The river tells the exiles that no place is too dead for the water that comes from God.

The verse that carries the intention is the one with the guide's question, 'Son of man, do you see this?', verse 6. He is asking Ezekiel to look and remember, and he wants him to tell the house of Israel what he has seen, as 40:4 commanded. The vision is addressed to a people who needed to hear that their story would not end in salt.

The second half of the chapter has a more practical intention. The tribes are to divide the land equally, verse 14, because God swore to give it to their fathers. The inheritance is no one's achievement. And the closing welcome of the foreigner in verses 22 to 23 shows the author expected a community with no second class: those who live among Israel and raise children there are given a share exactly like the native-born.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The river is something Ezekiel sees, not something he is told to build. The chapter describes a future act of God and does not command anything about rivers, trees or fisheries. Readers who try to find a literal stream running down to En-gedi miss what the text is trying to do, and so do readers who dismiss it as only a figure. The New Testament's use of the image shows that it points to the Spirit and to the new creation, John 7:38 and Revelation 22:1.

The borders and the allotments are more directly prescriptive, since they come as an instruction, 'you are to divide the land'. Yet they too sit inside a vision of the age to come, and the church does not take them as a command for any modern state. What does carry forward is the principle of fair shares, the refusal to treat any tribe as superior, and the rule that the resident foreigner be treated 'as native-born', which echoes Leviticus 19:34 and shapes how believers treat the stranger today.

debates.question: Is the river a literal future stream or a symbol fulfilled in Christ and the new creation?

views.label: A literal stream in a restored land
views.case: The vision gives measurements, place names such as En-gedi and En-eglaim, and a clear course to the Dead Sea. Those who hold a future literal Temple read it as an actual change to the geography of the land, much like the topographical changes in Zechariah 14:4 and 14:8.

views.label: A symbol of the Spirit and the life of the new creation
views.case: The water deepens without a tributary and trees bear fruit every month. The New Testament takes it as Christ's gift of the Spirit, John 7:37 to 39, and as the river of the water of life, Revelation 22:1 to 2. On this reading the river is a theological picture and the church already drinks from it.

debates.bearing: Both views agree that the river's source is God's presence and its effect is life. The New Testament's own use of the image shows its deepest meaning is not postponed.

debates.question: Why are the swamps and marshes left for salt, verse 11?

views.label: A sign that healing is not total
views.case: Some see in the exception a hint that judgment remains alongside mercy, or that places which refuse the river stay barren. The salt is the portion that remains for those not reached by the stream.

views.label: A practical provision
views.case: Others point out that salt was valuable in the ancient world and that the pans beside the sea would have supplied it. The vision, on this reading, leaves a resource in place and shows that new creation does not abolish usefulness.

debates.bearing: The text does not explain the exception, so confidence is not warranted. It does show that the picture is detailed and is not a naive claim that every place will look the same.

study.originalLanguages:
The most important word in verses 8 to 9 is hidden in English. The BSB says the water 'becomes fresh', but the footnote to verse 8 says the Hebrew is 'healed', and it adds 'also in verses 9 and 11'. The verb is rapha, 'to heal', the same root that gives marpe in verse 12, so the sea is healed by the river just as the leaves heal people. The same verb is God's name in Exodus 15:26, 'I am the LORD who heals you', and Naaman's skin is healed in Jordan in 2 Kings 5. Ezekiel makes the healing cosmic: salt water, not a body, is the patient.

The depth is told in body measures. The water comes up to the ankles, the knees and the waist, and then it is deep enough for swimming, a 'river that could not be crossed on foot', verse 5. The Hebrew phrase for the swimming water is literally 'waters of swimming'. The last stage is the one no measuring line can follow.

The verb for life in verse 9 is chayah, 'to live', and the BSB's 'flourish' translates it. The 'swarms of living creatures' in the same verse echo the language of Genesis 1:20, so the passage uses creation language: the sea becomes a place where living things teem again.

The trees in verse 12 bear 'each month', which is literally 'to its months'. The word for the leaves' use is marpe, 'healing', related to the verb above. The only other place where leaves heal is Revelation 22:2, where the leaves are 'for the healing of the nations'.

In 47:14 the land 'will fall to you', from the verb nafal, 'to fall', the verb of the lot, because inheritance was decided by lot, Numbers 26:55 and Joshua 14:2. In verse 22 the causative form of the same verb tells the people to 'allot' the land to the foreigners as well, so the same casting of the lot applies to both.

Finally, the foreigner is to be treated 'as native-born', ke'ezrach, and the phrase pairs with ger, as in Leviticus 24:22, 'the same standard of law for the foreign resident and the native'. The condition 'who have children', literally 'who have fathered sons among you', marks a family settled in the land and not a passing visitor.

typology.type: The river from beneath the temple threshold, 47:1
typology.fulfillment: A trickle from the threshold of God's house grows into a river with no tributary, which points to the Spirit given through Christ. Jesus stood at the Feast of Booths and said, 'Streams of living water will flow from within him', John 7:37 to 39, and promised the Samaritan woman 'a fount of water springing up to eternal life', John 4:14. The correspondence is water flowing from God's dwelling; the escalation is that the dwelling is now Christ and His people, 1 Corinthians 3:16. At the cross, 'blood and water' flowed from His side, John 19:34. The type falls short in that the vision's water flows from a building, while the Spirit now flows from living hearts.

The most lifeless water in the land is healed and filled with fish. This is a picture of regeneration. Ezekiel had already promised 'a new heart and a new spirit', 36:26 to 27, and Paul says 'if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation', 2 Corinthians 5:17. In the end, creation itself will be set free from its bondage, Romans 8:21. The type falls short because the vision keeps marshes for salt, while the final promise is that nothing accursed remains, Revelation 22:3.

typology.type: The trees with monthly fruit and healing leaves, 47:12
typology.fulfillment: The trees are fed by the water from the sanctuary and so never fail. Psalm 1:3 had pictured the righteous man as a tree by streams of water that yields fruit in its season, and Revelation 22:2 sees the tree of life by the river 'bearing twelve kinds of fruit and yielding a fresh crop for each month'. The correspondence is life that depends on the water from God's presence; the escalation is that the tree of life, barred in Genesis 3:24, is now freely accessible. The leaves for 'the healing of the nations' reach beyond Israel to all peoples.

typology.type: The foreigner given an inheritance, 47:22 to 23
typology.fulfillment: The stranger is no longer a guest but an heir, placed in a tribe and given land. Paul says that Gentiles who were 'strangers to the covenants of the promise' are now 'fellow citizens with the saints', Ephesians 2:12 to 19, and 'if you belong to Christ, then you are Abraham's seed and heirs according to the promise', Galatians 3:29. The type falls short because Ezekiel's foreigner still receives a plot inside Israel's tribes, whereas in Christ the nations are gathered into a new people whose inheritance is the whole earth, Matthew 5:5.

study.christ:
The river leads to Christ most directly through John 7. The scene is the last day of the Feast of Booths, in which the Temple's water ceremony was observed, and Jesus calls out an invitation to the thirsty to come to Him and drink, promising that streams of living water will flow from within the one who believes, John 7:37 to 38. John adds, 'He was speaking about the Spirit, whom those who believed in Him were later to receive', John 7:39. The Temple was the place the river came from in Ezekiel; now Jesus claims to be that place and the source of the water. John 2:21 has already said He spoke of the temple of His body.

The cross is the place where the river is first seen flowing. When the soldier pierced Jesus' side, 'immediately blood and water flowed out', John 19:34. John does not say this is Ezekiel 47, but his Gospel has been setting Jesus beside the Temple and its water from the beginning, and the placement of water at the moment of death is hard to miss. The Spirit is given after the glorification, John 7:39, and Ezekiel 36:25 to 27 had tied the cleansing water to the gift of a new heart and the Spirit.

The river leads to Christ also by its fulfilment in Revelation. The water of life flows 'from the throne of God and of the Lamb', Revelation 22:1. The Lamb stands at the source. The trees and their leaves for healing, the monthly fruit, and the absence of curse all attach to the Lamb's throne.

The foreigner's inheritance leads to Christ too. In Him 'there is neither Jew nor Greek', Galatians 3:28, and those once far away are brought near, Ephesians 2:13. Jesus is the cornerstone of a building in which Gentiles are fitted together, Ephesians 2:20 to 22.

A caution keeps the reading honest. The names En-gedi and En-eglaim, the thousand-cubit measures and the exact borders are not hidden portraits of Jesus. The New Testament takes up the river, the tree and the welcome, and these are the lines on which the passage leads to Christ.
study.god:
The chapter shows a God whose presence is a source, not only a boundary. In chapters 40 to 46 the sanctuary is full of fences, gates and measures that keep people at a respectful distance. Here the same house becomes the origin of something that goes out to the world. The holy God does not hoard His holiness; it overflows. The water that starts under the threshold is the first sign that His presence is meant to bless beyond itself.

He is a God who gives life where there is none. The Sea in verse 8 is as dead as water gets, and He heals it. This is the same power that made the dry bones of chapter 37 live, and it is why Ezekiel's God is called the God who gives life to the dead, as Romans 4:17 later says of Abraham's God. Nothing is too ruined for Him, and He starts with a trickle and does not rush.

He is a God who keeps His oath. The land comes 'because I swore with an uplifted hand to give it to your forefathers', verse 14. The promise to Abraham, Genesis 15:18, has not lapsed through the exile, and He will bring it to its end. At the same time He is a God of equal shares, who tells the tribes to divide the land equally among them, verse 14, with no favourite.

He is also a God who welcomes the stranger. He tells them to give foreigners an inheritance and to treat them as native-born, verses 22 to 23, and He puts this into His own mouth: 'declares the Lord GOD'. Leviticus 19:34 had already told Israel to love the foreigner as themselves because they had been foreigners in Egypt. In this verse the welcome is made concrete in land.

For worship, the river invites us to drink and to carry what we receive. A people who have been given water that never stops are meant to stand where others can reach it. The chapter teaches us to praise a God who gives more than we asked, measure by measure, until it can no longer be crossed on foot.

crossReferences.note: A river flowed out of Eden to water the garden and then divided into four heads. Ezekiel 47:1 to 12 gives the Temple what the garden had: a river that waters trees and gives life. The vision takes the lost Eden and relocates it at the place where God dwells with His people.

A river whose streams delight the city of God, where the Most High dwells, is the psalmist's way of saying that God's presence is the source of joy and security. Jerusalem itself has no natural river, so the picture belongs with Ezekiel's: the water comes from the presence, not the landscape.

A spring flows from the house of the LORD to water the Valley of Acacias, a dry place east of Jerusalem. Joel and Ezekiel share the picture of a stream from the sanctuary that reaches a barren valley and makes it fruitful.

Living water flows out from Jerusalem toward the Eastern Sea and the Western Sea, in summer and winter alike. The two seas correspond to the Dead Sea and the Mediterranean, and the year-round flow answers the leaves that do not wither in Ezekiel 47:12.

Jesus stands at the Feast of Booths and offers living water to the thirsty, and John interprets it as the Spirit. This is the New Testament's clearest use of Ezekiel's image, with the believer becoming the place from which the river now flows.

God promises to sprinkle clean water on His people and give them a new heart and His Spirit. The water here is the inward counterpart to the river of chapter 47, and the two passages together say that life flows from God and is received in the heart.

The river of the water of life flows from the throne of God and of the Lamb, with the tree of life on either side, giving fruit each month and leaves for the healing of the nations. John gathers every element of Ezekiel 47:12 and moves the source from the Temple to the throne.

The Torah's borders of the land set the pattern for Ezekiel 47:15 to 20. The two lists agree on much of the north and south but Ezekiel places the Jordan as the eastern edge for all twelve tribes, so that no one stays on the far side.

The foreigner living among Israel is to be treated as native-born and loved as oneself, because Israel was once a foreigner in Egypt. Ezekiel 47:22 carries this from attitude to land: the foreigner receives an inheritance among the tribes.

Gentiles who were separate from Christ, alienated from the commonwealth of Israel and without hope have been brought near through the blood of Christ. Paul's words describe the status that Ezekiel 47:22 to 23 begins to reverse, and show how the welcome is finally realised.

study.oneStory:
The Bible's first picture of God's people is a garden with a river, Genesis 2:10, and its last is a city with a river, Revelation 22:1. Ezekiel 47 is the hinge between them. After Eden's river was lost to human sin, the next water the story gives is the water of Meribah, from a rock, and the water of Jordan, which Israel crossed to enter the land. Here at last is a water that comes from the presence of God and heals the world.

The chapter answers what came before it. The exile had left the land desolate and the people as dry bones. Chapter 36 had promised that the desolate land would become 'like the garden of Eden', 36:35, and chapter 37 had given breath to the bones. The river shows how: life flows from the house of God and reaches the most ruined place in the land. The chapter also answers the promise of the land, because the borders show the inheritance as a gift God swore to give.

What the chapter sets up is the New Testament's account of the Spirit and the church. Jesus offers living water to the thirsty, John 7:37 to 39, the Spirit is poured out at Pentecost, and the gospel goes outward from Jerusalem to the nations. The foreigner who is given a share in the land becomes the Gentile who is made a fellow citizen, Ephesians 2:19, and the promise to Abraham that all nations would be blessed, Genesis 12:3, comes into view.

The story ends with the river's final form. In the new creation the river runs from the throne of God and of the Lamb, the tree of life is back, the curse is gone, and the leaves heal the nations, Revelation 22:1 to 3. The land, the temple and the river that Ezekiel saw in outline are brought together in a world where 'the earth will be full of the knowledge of the LORD as the sea is full of water', Isaiah 11:9.

quiz.q: What happens to the water's depth as the man measures it eastward from the temple, with no tributary joining it?

options.text: It deepens progressively from ankle-deep to knee-deep to waist-deep to an uncrossable river
options.note: 47:3-5 traces exactly this progression, deepening with no visible source but the temple itself.

options.text: It stays the same shallow depth the entire distance measured
options.note: The text explicitly describes continual deepening at each thousand-cubit measurement.

options.text: It grows shallower the farther it flows from the temple
options.note: The opposite occurs; the river deepens as it moves away from its source.

options.text: It splits into several smaller streams as it flows east
options.note: No splitting is described; it remains a single river that keeps deepening.

quiz.q: What effect does the river have on the Dead Sea, called here simply 'the Sea'?

options.text: The water there becomes fresh, teeming with swarms of living creatures and many fish
options.note: 47:8-9 describes this transformation of the notoriously lifeless Dead Sea.

options.text: It causes the Sea to dry up completely
options.note: The opposite happens; the Sea is filled with fresh, life-sustaining water.

options.text: It has no effect on the Sea at all, only on the land around it
options.note: 47:8 states directly that the water flowing into the Sea makes it fresh.

options.text: It turns the Sea into dry, arable farmland
options.note: The text describes the Sea becoming fresh water full of fish, not land.

quiz.q: What are the leaves of the river's fruit trees used for, according to 47:12?

options.text: Healing
options.note: 47:12 states plainly that the leaves are for healing, language Revelation 22:2 later echoes directly.

options.text: Weaving baskets for the temple
options.note: No such use is mentioned; the text specifies healing as the leaves' purpose.

options.text: Nothing; only the fruit is useful
options.note: The text explicitly gives the leaves a purpose distinct from the fruit, healing.

options.text: Fuel for the temple's sacrificial fires
options.note: The stated use of the leaves is healing, not fuel.

quiz.q: Who, in addition to native-born Israelites, is promised a full inheritance among the tribes in 47:22-23?

options.text: Foreigners who dwell among Israel and have children there, treated as native-born
options.note: 47:22 states this explicitly, an inheritance for these foreigners as if they were native Israelites.

options.text: No one else; the inheritance is strictly limited to the twelve tribes by blood
options.note: The text explicitly widens the inheritance to include settled foreigners as well.

options.text: Only the priests and Levites receive any additional portion here
options.note: This passage addresses foreigners specifically, not priestly allotments, which were fixed earlier in chapters 44-45.

options.text: Only foreigners who first renounce all family ties in their homeland
options.note: The text's condition is dwelling among Israel and having children there, not renouncing prior family ties.

quiz.q: How does Jesus' invitation in John 7:37-39 draw on the imagery of Ezekiel 47?

options.text: Jesus promises that streams of living water, referring to the Spirit, will flow from within all who believe in Him, echoing the river of life flowing from God's presence
options.note: John 7:37-39 records this invitation, which the New Testament and Revelation 22:1-2 tie directly to imagery like Ezekiel's river.

options.text: Jesus warns that no one may drink from the temple's water without priestly permission
options.note: This is the opposite of Jesus' open invitation, 'let him come to Me and drink.'

options.text: Jesus limits this promise only to the priests of Zadok's line
options.note: Jesus' invitation is addressed broadly, 'if anyone is thirsty,' not restricted to a priestly line.

options.text: Jesus reinterprets the river as referring only to physical, literal water for drinking
options.note: John clarifies that Jesus spoke of the Spirit, not merely literal water, John 7:39.

questions: The river deepens with no tributary in sight, growing entirely from what flows out of God's own presence. Where in your life have you tried to generate spiritual life on your own instead of receiving it as a gift flowing from God?

The river makes even the Dead Sea fresh and full of life. Is there a part of your life, a relationship, a habit, a wound, that feels as lifeless as the Dead Sea, that you need to bring under the flow of God's presence rather than trying to fix on your own?

The trees along the river bear fruit every month without fail, because the water never stops flowing from the sanctuary. What would change in your life if you drew on Christ, the living water, continually rather than only in moments of crisis?

The settled foreigner receives a full inheritance alongside native-born Israel. Who in your life might you be tempted to treat as a permanent outsider, and how does this vision, and the gospel it anticipates, call you to welcome them instead?

Revelation 22 shows this river finally reaching its full, unending form, with a tree whose leaves heal the nations. How does picturing that final scene shape the hope you carry into hard seasons of waiting right now?

translationNotes.note: An embedded line break in the source text between 'knee-deep water' and 'Again he measured' has been flattened into continuous prose here, matching the sentence's original sense.
'Deep enough for swimming' renders water too deep to wade through.
An embedded line break in the source text between 'This shall be the boundary of the land:' and 'On the north side' has been flattened into continuous prose here.
'Foreigners who dwell among you and who have children' reflects a settled, ongoing presence rather than a transient visitor, the basis on which this inheritance is granted.
